[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] The hour of day has a strongly non-monotonic effect: overnight hours (blue, low values) push predicted demand very far down, while certain daytime hours (red/orange, higher values) raise it above the baseline — the widest swing of any feature. The exact peak hour cannot be pinpointed from this plot alone, but the positive contributions clearly come from the higher-value hours.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the most important feature, with a spread from roughly −3 to +1.3 in log space — larger than all other features combined.

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] Higher temperatures (red dots) are associated with contributions near zero to slightly positive, while lower temperatures (blue dots) pull predicted demand down substantially, reaching around −1.5 in log space. The relationship is roughly monotonic: warmer = more riders.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the second most important feature, with a large horizontal spread second only to hour of day.

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] Year acts as a simple step change: 2011 hours (blue) sit at a moderately negative contribution and 2012 hours (red) sit at a moderately positive one, reflecting overall system growth from one year to the next.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the third most important feature, with a clearly visible but narrower spread than hour and temperature.

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Winter months (blue, low values) contribute slightly negatively and summer months (red, high values) contribute slightly positively, giving a roughly monotonic seasonal rise from January to the warmer months. The overall swing is modest, spanning roughly −0.3 to +0.2 in log space.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the fourth most important feature, with a noticeably smaller range than the top three.

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] Higher humidity (red dots) tends to sit on the negative side of the contribution axis, while low humidity (blue dots) is closer to zero, meaning wetter air is associated with reduced predicted demand. The effect is moderate in size, with most dots between about −0.5 and +0.1 and one extreme low-humidity outlier much further left.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the fifth most important feature, with a moderate spread comparable to month.

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Better weather (blue, low codes = clear skies) contributes near zero, while worse weather (red, high codes = rain or snow) pulls predicted demand down to around −0.5 in log space. The effect is a step-like decline as conditions worsen.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the sixth most important feature, with a modest but clearly directional spread.

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] The dots for all weekdays cluster very tightly around zero, with blue and red dots intermingled and no clear directional pattern. The effect of the day of the week on predicted demand is negligible in this model.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the seventh most important feature and is effectively negligible — its spread is tiny compared to all features above it.

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] Higher wind speeds (red dots) sit slightly on the negative side (down to roughly −0.3), while low wind speeds (blue) are near zero, meaning stronger winds modestly reduce predicted demand. The overall effect is small.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the eighth most important feature, with a very small spread and only a minor influence on predictions.

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] Both holiday and non-holiday hours cluster almost exactly at zero, with essentially no horizontal spread. The model treats holidays as having a negligible effect on predicted hourly demand.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the least important feature and can be considered negligible for planning purposes.

[RECOMMENDATION] Focus operational planning — bike availability and staffing — primarily on the hour of day and temperature, as these two features drive the vast majority of demand variation; ensure full availability during warm-weather daytime hours and scale back overnight and in cold conditions.
